projects.title: Kiwi Swerve Drivetrain
projects.summary: An affordable drivetrain with three modules that can move in any direction and is practical for competitions or teaching.

overview.problem: Competition swerve drives often need four modules, specialized parts, and a large budget. That makes them difficult for smaller teams to build and maintain.
overview.method: I used three steerable pods, chose parts that were easy to find, and handled steering accuracy with encoders and Python running on a Raspberry Pi.
overview.result: The first robot proved that the layout could move smoothly in any direction with three modules, less power, and less expensive hardware. It also gave me a solid starting point for version two.

sections.heading: First Robot
sections.body: This prototype was my first test of the Kiwi swerve idea using three modules. What I learned from it became the starting point for the next version.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: The Kiwi swerve drivetrain is an affordable system that can move in any direction and is easy to maintain. It uses three modules instead of four, along with common mechanical parts and continuous rotation servos with encoder feedback. I also built a custom electronics stack and wrote the Python controls so the system would be useful for both competitions and robotics education.

sections.heading: First Prototype Build
sections.body: The first prototype uses common gears and bearings sourced from Amazon and ServoCity, making its pods less expensive and easier to replace. Its structure combines parts made with 3D printing, plates made with CNC machining, and standard hardware. Each module uses a servo that can rotate continuously, along with an encoder for steering feedback. An HTD5 belt connects the servo to the pod. The drive motor uses a longer, lighter HTD2 belt, allowing the motor and steering servo to remain stationary while the pod turns freely.

sections.heading: Electronics
sections.body: A Raspberry Pi anchors the custom electronics stack. Each drive motor uses a motor driver rated for 10 amps, steering is managed through a servo HAT, and an encoder board with 12 bit resolution provides precise angle feedback for every module. These common, maintainable components keep the system accessible and easy to modify.

sections.heading: Programming
sections.body: Python software running on the Raspberry Pi implements Kiwi swerve kinematics and translates driver or autonomous commands into coordinated motion across all three modules. The steering controller continuously compares encoder feedback with the target angle and corrects the servos in real time for smooth, predictable movement. The software also synchronizes steering and drive motion to keep modules aligned and minimize unnecessary power draw.

sections.heading: Second Robot: V2 in Progress
sections.body: The second Kiwi swerve robot is currently in development. This next version will build on the first prototype’s mechanical design, electronics, and software control system.

projects.title: AI Eye Animatronic Chatbot
projects.summary: A voice activated AI assistant that can hold a conversation while moving an expressive animatronic eye.

overview.problem: Voice assistants can sound responsive while still feeling physically disconnected, and adding moving hardware introduces noise that can disrupt listening.
overview.method: I paired a compact eye mechanism that moves across two axes with linked eyelids and conversational software. I then coordinated the motion and microphone states so the eye never competed with speech input.
overview.result: The finished prototype can talk, listen, and react with smooth eye movements. The servos also stay quiet enough that they do not interfere with normal conversation.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: The goal was to create a lifelike assistant activated by voice that could listen and respond naturally. It also needed to control an expressive mechanical eye without letting servo noise interfere with speech recognition.

sections.heading: Mechanical Design
sections.body: Two hidden servos move the eye vertically and horizontally from a compact mechanism mounted to a monitor arm. Linked upper and lower eyelids create synchronized expressions, while reinforced pivots keep the movement stable and repeatable.

sections.heading: Controls
sections.body: The software combines wake word detection, speech recognition, and ChatGPT conversation. Cosine easing smooths eye and eyelid movement, coordinated states manage blinking and attention, and the servos pause while the microphone is listening to reduce noise.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The completed prototype can wake, listen, converse, interrupt, and reset in real time. Smooth eye motion and synchronized blinking give the assistant a more natural presence while preserving reliable voice interaction.

projects.title: Coaxial Swerve Drive
projects.summary: A compact FTC swerve module designed to use accessible parts and work with several common hardware systems.

overview.problem: Most swerve modules sized for FTC are difficult to fit inside a robot, expensive to reproduce, and limited to a small set of proprietary parts.
overview.method: I built and compared two compact coaxial pod designs, using the first to prove the geometry and the second to prioritize common parts and multiple mounting standards.
overview.result: The second design stayed compact but became cheaper to repair and easier for teams to adapt to the hardware they already use.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: Traditional FTC swerve modules can be too large and expensive for many teams. This project explored a compact, maintainable coaxial pod that could fit inside a competition robot without requiring specialized components.

sections.heading: First Prototype
sections.body: The first design fit inside a cube measuring four inches on each side and combined a printed structure with shafts, gears, and bearings. The drivetrain used four pods with one motor and one servo per module, proving the steering and drive arrangement worked as a complete chassis.

sections.heading: Second Prototype
sections.body: The second version replaced expensive specialty hardware with generic Amazon and AliExpress parts. The module changed from an L shape to a rectangular pod, added mounting support for GoBilda, REV, and AndyMark systems, and grew by less than a quarter inch.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The first pod worked but cost about $350, putting the full chassis near $1,300. The second design substantially reduced cost while improving compatibility and serviceability, creating a stronger foundation for continued development.

projects.title: Simple Swerve Drive
projects.summary: A differential swerve chassis designed around an FTC budget, size rules, and hardware that many teams already use.

overview.problem: Differential swerve gives a robot great mobility, but the gearing, size, and number of parts make it a difficult FTC project.
overview.method: I simplified a proven differential layout, embedded bearings directly in the gears, and repeatedly repackaged the motors until the chassis fit the legal envelope.
overview.result: The finished two pod chassis can be built around either REV or GoBILDA hardware, and all four CAD versions are saved in the project repository.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: After the 2023 to 2024 NYC FTC championship, the goal was to build a swerve robot between competition seasons despite the complexity, packaging constraints, and cost that make swerve uncommon in FTC.

sections.heading: Development
sections.body: The design began with a study of differential swerve and a simplified version of FTC 11115's approach. The gearbox was reengineered around M3x45 bolts and bearings embedded in the gears, reducing specialized hardware while preserving the core mechanism.

sections.heading: Chassis Iteration
sections.body: The first layout measured 18.25 inches, so the motors were rotated 90 degrees with REV Ultra 90 gearboxes to meet FTC sizing. The chassis used two pods, omni wheels at the other corners, and space for a slide mechanism. Version two added cheaper configurations for REV Ultraplanetary and GoBilda Yellow Jacket motors.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The project is complete. The repository now preserves the full explanation, development images, and four downloadable CAD packages without depending on the former portfolio page or GrabCAD.

projects.title: FTC 9384 Robot: EggWUUUHH
projects.summary: Team 9384's CENTERSTAGE robot, improved through four versions to score pixels, launch a plane, and climb reliably.

overview.problem: CENTERSTAGE combined intake, precise backdrop scoring, launching, and climbing in one robot, leaving little room for a mechanism that could not evolve during the season.
overview.method: Our team treated the machine as a sequence of testable subsystems and revised the chassis, lift, intake, outtake, and endgame hardware as match feedback exposed weaknesses.
overview.result: After four revisions, we had a reliable competition robot that could complete every major part of the game.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: The CENTERSTAGE season required one robot to collect and score pixels on the backdrop, launch a paper plane, and climb at the end of a match. The team needed a design that could evolve rapidly throughout the season.

sections.heading: Core Systems
sections.body: The robot used a custom mecanum chassis made from sheet aluminum, a lift built from stacked drawer slides with printed spacers and pulleys, and an active intake with three stages. The backdrop outtake evolved through multiple pivot and pincher designs as testing exposed alignment and reliability issues.

sections.heading: Endgame and Autonomous
sections.body: A plane launcher powered by a spring handled the season's launch task, while an autonomous pixel pincher improved repeatable placement. The final climbing system paired a winch with pivoting hooks and passive rubber assistance.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: Across four major revisions, the team produced a reliable competition platform with strong slide, intake, outtake, launcher, and climber systems. The complete CAD and engineering portfolio document the full iteration process.

projects.title: Tubba Odometry Pods
projects.summary: A dead wheel tracking system that we used in competition before compact FTC odometry pods were easy to buy.

overview.problem: We needed dependable position tracking for autonomous routines and driver assistance, but compact FTC odometry pods were not common yet. The available options were expensive, hard to fit, or still required teams to design part of the mechanism themselves.
overview.method: I designed a compact pod with a passive omni wheel measuring 2 inches in diameter and an encoder with a hollow bore. I built the plates, shaft support, preload system, and mounts around Team 9384's chassis, then helped calibrate the pods as part of the robot's localization system.
overview.result: The completed pods were installed on EggWUUUHH and used successfully in competition. They tracked the robot consistently, strengthened autonomous path accuracy, and provided position feedback that could also support corrections during teleop driving.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: Reliable odometry required far more than attaching an encoder to a wheel. The complete module had to fit inside the robot, maintain dependable contact with the field, minimize sideways scrub, protect the sensor, and return repeatable measurements through impacts, fast direction changes, and an entire competition match.

sections.heading: Core System
sections.body: At its center, each pod used a REV encoder with a hollow bore and a passive AndyMark Dualie omni wheel measuring 2 inches in diameter. The tracking wheel rotated independently from the drivetrain, allowing the localization software to measure the robot's actual movement instead of estimating position only from the motion and slip of powered wheels.

sections.heading: Designed From Scratch
sections.body: Since there was no complete commercial solution that met our requirements, I designed the plates, shaft arrangement, bearings, wheel support, preload system, and chassis mounting as one compact assembly. The finished pod fit between the parallel plates on EggWUUUHH and was documented as a complete STEP assembly with individual manufacturing files.

sections.heading: Cost and Accessibility
sections.body: Each pod cost about $100 in 2024. The encoder was the most expensive part, while the rest used a printed frame, a standard omni wheel, common bearings, shaft stock, tubing, and regular fasteners. This kept the design practical to repair and reproduce.

sections.heading: Competition Result
sections.body: We installed and calibrated the pods on our competition robot, where they made autonomous movement more repeatable. The live position estimate also gave the control system useful feedback during driver control. Most importantly, the team could trust the readings during a match.

projects.title: FTC 9384 Robot: Crabby
projects.summary: Team 9384's POWERPLAY robot, rebuilt three times to score cones faster and make the chassis more stable.

overview.problem: POWERPLAY rewarded rapid cone cycles at several heights, so lift speed, turret accuracy, and drivetrain rigidity all had to improve together.
overview.method: We rebuilt the robot through three major configurations, replacing flexible or slow mechanisms with rigid slides, a claw, reinforced structure, and a more capable turret.
overview.result: The final robot was lower, stronger, and more consistent. Each major change came from a problem we saw during testing or competition.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: POWERPLAY required the robot to collect cones and place them on junction poles at several heights. Fast cycling, accurate alignment, and chassis stability were all critical to competitive performance.

sections.heading: Early Designs
sections.body: The first version paired REV linear slides with an H pattern mecanum chassis and a dual compliant wheel intake. Later iterations increased lift speed, replaced the roller intake with a claw, and introduced a direct drive turret supported by a lazy susan bearing.

sections.heading: Final Revision
sections.body: The final robot used dual rigid slides, an internal bevel gearbox chassis, a larger turret, and a reinforced frame. These changes addressed flex, speed, and alignment problems found during competition testing.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: Three major design cycles produced a polished FTC machine with a stable drivetrain that had a low profile, a fast lift, a reliable claw, and a precise turret. The project gave me direct experience turning match feedback into mechanical improvements.

projects.title: ZeroG Hydra 3D Printer
projects.summary: A large CoreXY printer built around print quality, automatic calibration, useful sensors, and dependable hardware.

overview.problem: Printers with a large build area often trade consistency and serviceability for volume or headline speed, especially when calibration still depends on manual adjustment.
overview.method: I centered the design on a rigid CoreXY frame, automatic bed alignment at three points, modular electronics, and a toolhead with several sensors for more repeatable extrusion.
overview.result: The Hydra is still in progress, but the main motion system, calibration setup, and monitoring hardware are working and ready for continued development.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: After building and modifying several printers, I wanted to make a larger machine that prioritized print quality, strong hardware, and reliable sensors instead of chasing speed alone.

sections.heading: Motion and Bed
sections.body: The Hydra uses a CoreXY motion system and a floating bed that pivots independently at three points. Each point can adjust during automatic tramming, creating a rigid platform while letting the firmware correct alignment before a print.

sections.heading: Electronics and Toolhead
sections.body: An electronics bay under the printer houses the USB hub, controller, power supply, solid state relay for the bed powered by 110 volts, and the Linux computer running Klipper. A Filimetrix design inspired the toolhead, which adds dual filament sensors, a cutter, Beacon eddy current probing, lighting, a touchscreen, a Phaetus Rapido hotend, and a Clockwork 2 extruder.

sections.heading: Status
sections.body: The printer is still in development. Its large build volume, automatic calibration, toolhead sensors, and extrusion system already make it the most ambitious printer I have built.

projects.title: Delta 3D Printer
projects.summary: A fast delta printer rebuilt with closed loop motion, direct drive extrusion, and a powerful CPAP cooling system.

overview.problem: The delta frame could move quickly, but friction, cooling limitations, and difficult calibration kept that speed from producing consistently clean parts.
overview.method: I rebuilt the machine through several toolhead versions, moving to direct drive, motion with encoder feedback, stronger remote cooling, and a probing system that uses the nozzle.
overview.result: The rebuilt printer keeps the speed of a delta machine while producing more consistent parts with better extrusion, cooling, and calibration.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: The project set out to combine the speed of a delta printer with consistent print quality. I used stepper motors with encoder feedback, a lightweight effector, and strong part cooling while working through the calibration and packaging challenges unique to delta kinematics.

sections.heading: Development
sections.body: The TEVO Little Monster frame, power supply, and solid state relay became the foundation. An early Bowden setup introduced friction and surface artifacts, so later revisions moved to direct drive and a CPAP blower mounted to the frame that feeds the effector through a lightweight hose.

sections.heading: Toolhead Iterations
sections.body: Version two combined the ducts, hotend, extruder, and probe but exposed problems with airflow and the probe offset. Version three lowered the hotend and center of gravity, improved the ducts, and added a detachable nozzle probe. NEMA 17 motors with encoder feedback and a TFT35 KlipperScreen completed the control system.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The finished machine prints quickly and consistently. It combines reliable motion feedback, strong extrusion through a direct drive system, improved calibration, powerful cooling, and a custom user interface.

projects.title: Voron V0.2990
projects.summary: A compact Voron that I modified for higher flow, better cooling, safer operation, and easier maintenance.

overview.problem: The compact Voron platform was capable, but heat management, extrusion flow, monitoring, and access to electronics limited its speed and reliability over long periods.
overview.method: I upgraded the machine as one connected system, pairing a toolhead with higher flow with external cooling, enclosure sensors, filtration, failure monitoring, and wiring that is easy to service.
overview.result: The upgrades made this small printer faster, easier to maintain, and safer to monitor during long or demanding prints.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: Starting from the Voron platform designed by the community, I focused on finding performance bottlenecks and improving extrusion, cooling, monitoring, filtration, and service access.

sections.heading: Performance Upgrades
sections.body: A custom toolhead combines a stronger extruder and high flow hotend for printing around 225 to 350 mm/s with travel speeds up to 650 mm/s. An external 12032 fan increases part cooling without adding excessive moving mass.

sections.heading: Reliability and Usability
sections.body: The enclosure adds active carbon filtration, a chamber thermistor, reinforced panels with RGB lighting, upgraded hinges, and a camera for failure detection and timelapses. A filament runout and extrusion sensor monitors material flow, while a larger Mini12864 display improves local control.

sections.heading: Serviceability
sections.body: DIN rail electronics, a hinged rear electronics door, and a quiet Noctua cooling fan make maintenance and thermal management easier. Together, the modifications turn the compact printer into a faster, safer, and more dependable machine.

projects.title: Self Balancing Robot
projects.summary: Three affordable balancing robots built from parts at school to teach feedback control with Raspberry Pi and Arduino boards.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: The club wanted a practical controls project that could be built with parts already available at school. A robot that balances itself made gyroscope feedback, tuning, and motor control in real time visible and easy to experiment with.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Three robots were created: one controlled by a Raspberry Pi running Python and two based on Arduino Nano and Uno boards. Each used an existing motor driver, DC motors, and gyroscope inside a custom chassis.

sections.heading: Controls
sections.body: A PID controller uses a closed feedback loop to process the robot angle, synchronize both motors, and correct disturbances. Repeated tuning and changes to wheel placement, chassis geometry, and center of gravity improved stability across each platform.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: All three robots can balance while standing still or moving forward and backward. Club members could work directly with the robots while learning PID control, embedded programming, and the mechanical choices that affect stability.

projects.title: Crab Crawler
projects.summary: Three compact ESP32 walking robots built to teach wireless programming, sensors, and coordinated servo movement.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: The project needed to introduce ESP32 programming, camera feedback, sensors, and servo breakout boards through a robot simple enough for students to understand and modify.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Three compact crawlers were assembled from 3D printed frames, two servos per robot, an ESP32 CAM for wireless control and video, an OLED status display, and a dedicated servo driver.

sections.heading: Programming
sections.body: Custom code coordinates the walking gait, live display information, camera connection, and wireless commands. The gait and body geometry were tuned together to improve traction and keep the mechanism with two servos stable.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The crawlers can walk reliably, stream live video, and show their status in real time. Since they use few parts and straightforward code, students can understand them and add their own ideas.

projects.title: AutoCAD I
projects.summary: Introductory technical drafting work focused on accurate drawings, dimensions, layouts, and clear presentation.
projects.classRundown: Completed 2D drafting exercises, homework, quizzes, a midterm, and a final while practicing dimensions, title blocks, layouts, and plotting.

overview.problem: I needed to learn how to turn part geometry into technical drawings that were accurate, readable, and ready to print.
overview.method: I completed drawing exercises, homework, quizzes, a midterm, and a final while practicing dimensions, title blocks, layouts, and plotting.
overview.result: The course gave me a solid foundation in AutoCAD and made my drawings faster, cleaner, and easier to understand.

sections.heading: Coursework
sections.body: Classwork, homework, quizzes, a midterm, and a final helped me build a strong foundation in technical drafting.

sections.heading: Skills Developed
sections.body: The work covers 2D geometry, object snaps, repeated features, dimensioning, sheet layouts, title blocks, and plotting drawings to PDF.

projects.title: AutoCAD II
projects.summary: More advanced drafting work with inch and metric drawings, reusable title blocks, 3D geometry, and a final with several parts.
projects.classRundown: Created advanced inch and metric drawings, reusable title blocks, 3D geometry, revisions, and a multi-part final project.

overview.problem: The second AutoCAD course required more complex drawings, different unit systems, and a consistent format across several assignments.
overview.method: I worked through advanced exercises, reusable title blocks, 3D geometry, revisions, and a final project made up of several drawings.
overview.result: I became more comfortable organizing larger drawing sets and keeping the dimensions, layouts, and presentation consistent.

sections.heading: Coursework
sections.body: Chapter exercises, homework, assessments, and a staged final expanded the drafting workflow into more complex 2D and 3D work.

sections.heading: Skills Developed
sections.body: The work covers drawings with different unit systems, reusable title blocks, revisions, 3D geometry, and consistent presentation.

projects.title: Mastercam
projects.summary: Seven CAM tutorials that turned part geometry into simulated toolpaths and CNC programs.
projects.classRundown: Completed seven CAM tutorials covering stock setup, tool selection, milling operations, toolpath simulation, and posted CNC code.

overview.problem: I knew how to model parts in CAD, but I still needed to learn how those models become safe and organized CNC operations.
overview.method: I created stock setups, selected tools, programmed milling operations, simulated each toolpath, and posted the results as CNC code.
overview.result: The course taught me the complete CAM workflow and prepared me to apply those skills later on real CNC equipment.

sections.heading: Coursework
sections.body: This freshman course began with existing CAD experience and introduced the manufacturing decisions required to turn a digital model into CNC machine instructions.

sections.heading: Process
sections.body: Projects covered 2D and 3D machining strategies, toolpath creation, stock setup, feeds and speeds, tool selection, and simulation. Each assignment connected model geometry to the physical sequence a mill would follow.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The course helped me understand the complete CAD to CAM process and how design choices affect machining time, tool access, surface finish, and manufacturability.

projects.title: MATLAB
projects.summary: Programming assignments that used scripts, functions, matrices, and graphs to solve math and engineering problems.
projects.classRundown: Wrote scripts and reusable functions using matrices, imported data, engineering calculations, and plots across several class projects.

overview.problem: I needed to move beyond basic Python and learn a programming tool made for engineering calculations, data, and graphs.
overview.method: I wrote scripts and functions that used matrices, imported data, solved math problems, and created plots for several class projects.
overview.result: By the end of the course, I could use MATLAB to organize calculations, study data, and explain results with clear visualizations.

sections.heading: Coursework
sections.body: This freshman course built on my basic Python experience and introduced me to MATLAB, a programming environment designed for engineering. Assignments introduced a different syntax and a workflow built around numerical problem solving.

sections.heading: Computing Skills
sections.body: Projects used scripts and reusable functions to work with matrices, arrays, and structured calculations. MATLAB's numerical tools made it possible to analyze data and test mathematical relationships efficiently.

sections.heading: Application
sections.body: Plots and graphs made the results easier to read and explain. The course showed me how programming connects to mathematical models and engineering data.

projects.title: MECH 1101 Machine Shop
projects.summary: A team machining project that started with blank plate stock and ended with a drilled, finished, and inspected part.
projects.classRundown: Machined a plate from blank stock through layout, drilling, tapping, hole finishing, notching, filing, sanding, and final inspection.

overview.problem: Our team had to turn a blank metal plate into a finished part while learning how to work accurately and safely in the machine shop.
overview.method: We laid out the part, drilled and finished the holes, cut the notch, filed and sanded the edges, and inspected the final dimensions.
overview.result: The project gave me direct experience with common shop tools and showed how small errors during one step affect the final inspection.

sections.heading: Class Project
sections.body: The team converted blank metal plate stock into a dimensioned part with four hole treatments, a square notch, finished edges, and inspected dimensions.

sections.heading: Skills Developed
sections.body: The build documents layout, drilling, tapping, reaming, countersinking, counterboring, filing, sanding, and tolerance inspection.

projects.title: Autodesk Inventor
projects.summary: Parametric CAD coursework covering part models, assemblies, drawings, presentations, and finite element analysis.
projects.classRundown: Modeled parametric parts and assemblies, then created manufacturing drawings, exploded views, presentations, and a static stress analysis.

overview.problem: I wanted to build stronger parametric CAD skills and understand how separate parts, drawings, presentations, and simulations fit together.
overview.method: I modeled parts, constrained assemblies, created exploded views and manufacturing drawings, and completed a static stress analysis.
overview.result: The course improved how I organize larger CAD projects and gave me experience carrying a design from individual features to a documented assembly.

sections.heading: Coursework
sections.body: Homework, class projects, a midterm, a mini project, and a final cover part modeling, constrained assemblies, drawing production, and presentations.

sections.heading: Skills Developed
sections.body: The work includes modeling with parametric features, assembly constraints, exploded views, manufacturing drawings, revision history, and static stress analysis.

projects.title: CUNY Research: 3D Printing With Geopolymers
projects.summary: Summer 2025 research on geopolymer materials and a custom 3D printer built to extrude them.

sections.heading: Research
sections.body: During summer 2025 at New York City College of Technology, I worked on geopolymer mixtures that could be used as a printable construction material. The research included mixing materials, studying curing, evaluating samples, and testing the extrusion process.

sections.heading: Printer Development
sections.body: A custom 3D printer was designed and built to handle the material, joining mechanical design with experiments in flow, consistency, layer formation, and process control.

sections.heading: Recognition
sections.body: The work was presented at CUNY's Third Annual Celebrating Research Excellence Symposium and earned a Certificate of Research Achievement for completing and presenting two summer research projects.

projects.title: NSF Advanced Manufacturing Training
projects.summary: A manufacturing program lasting five weeks where I worked with microscopy, CNC machining, 3D printing, CAD, and technical presentations.

sections.heading: Program
sections.body: During freshman year, I attended the NSF Advanced Manufacturing Summer Training Camp for five weeks. The program introduced a broad range of equipment and professional engineering practices.

sections.heading: Technical Experience
sections.body: I worked with electron microscopes, CNC mills, 3D printers, SolidWorks, and Autodesk Inventor. The program showed how inspection, modeling, machining, and additive manufacturing fit into one production process.

sections.heading: Communication
sections.body: Weekly video updates and presentations helped me get better at documenting technical work, explaining decisions, and sharing progress in a professional format.
